text: Unlike Windows, there's no single update command across all of Linux, because there's no single Linux — there are distributions, split into families by which package manager they use. The Debian family, including Ubuntu, uses APT and dot-deb packages. The Red Hat family, including RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux, and Fedora, uses YUM or its modern successor DNF, working with dot-rpm packages instead.

On a Debian-family system, patching is two distinct steps, and the order matters. apt update doesn't install anything at all — it only refreshes the local package index, the list of what's available in each repository. apt upgrade then installs newer versions of packages already on the system, without removing anything. Run upgrade without update first, and apt may be working off a stale index. full-upgrade behaves the same way but is allowed to remove a package if dependencies require it.

On a Red Hat-family system, the same job is typically one command instead of two. yum update, or the newer dnf upgrade, refreshes repository metadata and installs available updates together, rather than splitting that into apt's two steps. If an administrator just wants to see what's available first, yum check-update is the equivalent of running apt update alone — it lists updates without touching the system.

Both families support fully automatic patching, so a human isn't running these commands by hand on every machine. unattended-upgrades handles that on Debian and Ubuntu; dnf-automatic is the Red Hat-family equivalent. Both typically install only security-classified updates on a schedule. That closes the patch gap automatically, but it also removes the manual testing checkpoint — the same speed-versus-stability tension from Patch Tuesday, just automated instead of eliminated.

Patching closes known vulnerabilities, but someone still has to decide which ones matter most and in what order. That's what a published vulnerability identifier and a severity score are actually for. Next, what a CVE really is, what CVSS measures, and how an analyst turns that score into an actual patch priority.
